stem: What was the main aim of the Non-Aligned Movement during the Cold War?

options.content: To join NATO as a group
options.rationale: NATO was a Western bloc alliance.

options.content: To avoid joining either Cold War bloc
options.rationale: Correct: neither the US-led nor the Soviet-led bloc.
NAM opposed colonialism.

options.content: To support the Warsaw Pact against the West
options.rationale: The Warsaw Pact was the Eastern bloc alliance.

explanation: NAM members refused to join **either bloc** and opposed colonialism and apartheid.

stem: What was set up at the NAM summit in Harare in 1986?

stem: Why did Zimbabwe leave the Commonwealth in December 2003?

options.content: It was expelled at the Lusaka meeting

options.rationale: Correct: the government then withdrew.

explanation: Suspended in March 2002, Zimbabwe withdrew when the **Abuja CHOGM** of December 2003 kept the suspension.

stem: Which is the strongest criticism of the Non-Aligned Movement?

stem: The Commonwealth Secretariat was set up in London in 1965.

State **five** aims of the Non-Aligned Movement.

points.description: Independence from the Cold War blocs.
End colonialism.
End racism and apartheid.
World peace and disarmament.
Economic development / fairer world economy / sovereignty and self-determination.

stem: Describe the role of the Commonwealth in the events that led to Zimbabwe's independence.

points.description: Commonwealth members condemned UDI / supported sanctions.
Lusaka CHOGM, August 1979.
African leaders (Kaunda, Nyerere) argued the Patriotic Front must be included.
Agreed Britain should hold an all-party conference and supervised elections.
This led to the Lancaster House Conference (September-December 1979).
Commonwealth monitoring force and observers at the 1980 ceasefire and elections.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Commonwealth members condemned UDI and supported sanctions against Rhodesia. At the Lusaka CHOGM in August 1979, African leaders such as Kaunda and Nyerere argued that any settlement had to include the Patriotic Front, and the meeting agreed that Britain should call an all-party conference with supervised elections. This led to the Lancaster House Conference. A Commonwealth force then monitored the ceasefire, and Commonwealth observers watched the 1980 elections.

hints: Start with Lusaka 1979 and follow it through to 1980.

stem: Explain **two** functions of organs of the Commonwealth.

points.description: Names an organ (e.g. CHOGM).
Explains its function (leaders set policy every two years).
Names a second organ (e.g. Secretariat / CMAG).
Explains its function (organises programmes / deals with violations, can recommend suspension).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: CHOGM brings Commonwealth leaders together, normally every two years, to agree policy, as at Lusaka in 1979. The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group deals with serious violations of Commonwealth values such as the Harare Declaration and can recommend suspending a member.

explanation: Two marks per organ and function.
hints: CHOGM, the Secretariat and CMAG are the main organs.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a statement by a fictional Zimbabwean government spokesperson, December 2003 (invented for this question)

> The Commonwealth has become a club in which Britain and its friends punish those who take back their land. We will not beg to be readmitted. Zimbabwe's friends are in Africa and in the South.

**Source B** — a comment by a fictional Commonwealth human rights campaigner, December 2003 (invented for this question)

> The members agreed in Harare in 1991 to uphold democracy and human rights. Keeping the suspension simply holds a member to the promises it once hosted. The door remains open.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: According to Source A, why was Zimbabwe being punished?

points.description: For taking back its land (land reform).
By Britain and its friends using the Commonwealth.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How do Sources A and B differ in their explanation of Zimbabwe's suspension? Use details from both.

points.description: A: punishment for land reform.
B: enforcing democracy and human rights commitments.
A: Commonwealth controlled by Britain and friends.
B: commitments agreed by all members at Harare in 1991; door open.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use your own knowledge to explain why the two sources give different views.

points.description: A: government spokesperson defending its policy and dignity.
A: context of land reform and Western criticism; presenting a South/Africa alignment.
B: campaigner committed to the Harare Declaration.
B: context of the disputed 2002 election and suspension in March 2002.
Both selective: A omits election and rights concerns; B omits land and colonial history.
Judgement on why they differ (purpose and position).

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant factors or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Source A is from a government spokesperson, whose job was to defend government policy. After the suspension in March 2002, which followed the disputed presidential election, the government presented the Commonwealth's action as Britain's punishment for land reform, and pointed to friends in Africa and the developing world.

Source B is from a human rights campaigner, who supports the Harare Declaration of 1991, so he presents the suspension as holding Zimbabwe to democratic commitments it had hosted.

Each is selective: Source A does not mention concerns about the election and rights, while Source B says nothing about the land question and colonial history. They differ because of their authors' positions and purposes.

parts.explanation: Explain differences through provenance and context.

explanation: Source-based practice question on Zimbabwe and the Commonwealth (12 marks).
hints: Each source was written by someone with a clear point of view.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the origins of the Non-Aligned Movement.

points.description: Cold War divided the world into two blocs after 1945.
Newly independent states did not want to be drawn in.
Bandung Conference, April 1955 (29 Asian and African states).
Belgrade summit, September 1961 (Tito, Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How far was the Non-Aligned Movement successful in achieving its aims?

points.description: Success: collective voice for developing countries at the UN.
Success: kept colonialism and apartheid on the agenda; support for liberation; AFRICA Fund (Harare 1986).
Limit: no power to enforce; could not stop Cold War conflicts.
Limit: some members close to one bloc; economic aims (fairer world economy) largely unmet.
Supported judgement.

Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.
One or two relevant but undeveloped points.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
NAM had real successes. It gave newly independent countries a collective voice, especially at the UN, where they formed a majority. It kept colonialism and apartheid on the world agenda and supported liberation movements; at Harare in 1986 it set up the AFRICA Fund to help the Frontline States.

But its limits were serious. It had no means of enforcing decisions and could not stop Cold War conflicts that affected its members. Some members, such as Cuba, were in practice close to one bloc, which weakened its claim to independence. Its call in the 1970s for a fairer world economy achieved little.

Overall NAM succeeded as a voice for anti-colonialism and developing countries, but it was only partly successful because it lacked the power to change the policies of the superpowers or the world economy.
